author: Christian Metzger
title: Wallingford's historic Yale Homestead to be reassembled after 25 years in storage - NewsBreak
text:
By Christian Metzger ,
1 days ago The Yale Homestead, residence of the famous Yale family, was built in the 1790s. It was taken down in 2000 to make room for commercial development, but the Wallingford Historic Preservation Trust plans to rebuild it. (Wallingford Historic Preservation Trust) WALLINGFORD — The historic Yale Homestead may rise again in Wallingford , 25 years after it was taken down.
The state’s bond commission recently approved $500,000 for the Wallingford Historic Preservation Trust to reconstruct the centuries-old building, the first major step towards its restoration since it was disassembled in 2000 from 1055 N. Colony Road.
“The Yale Homestead is a treasured historic asset, and this funding will help preserve an important piece of our community’s heritage for future generations," state Sen. Paul Cicarella, R-North Haven, said in a statement. "By investing in restoration now, we can prevent more costly repairs in the future and protect taxpayers from significantly higher expenses down the road."
The Yale Homestead is a building with significant historical ties to the community’s history, said Jerry Ferrell Jr., president of WHPT. It was built in the 1790s by the first cousins of Elihu Yale, who gave his name to Yale University in New Haven. As Elihu had no children, those who inhabited the home were his closest relatives. The family is also the namesake for Yalesville, the unincorporated village within Wallingford.
It stayed in the family for more than a century, until it was sold in the 1940s. The homestead remained until the land was developed into a Home Depot. A condition of the land sale in the 1990s was the developer had to preserve the structure, and agreed to help pay to relocate it.
The homestead was one of the few remaining 18th century farmhouses left in the area at the time, and when the land was purchased by community member George Mesite, who owned the Silversmith restaurant, he ensured the home would be taken into the care of the WHPT.
The WHPT had the home disassembled piece by piece and stored in the back of four trailer trucks, where it has remained. While the trust said it intended to rebuild the structure in 2000, the opportunity never presented itself until now.
Ferrell credits that opportunity to Cicarella, who advocated for the funding to be allocated for the historic home's restoration.
"We want to thank Senator Cicarella for going to bat with the legislature and the governor and bringing these funds to Wallingford," Ferrell said. "$500,000 is a big boost to this project."
Though portions of the home were modernized over the course of its use, Farrell said the funding would allow them to reconstruct the home, reassembling it with the same 18th century techniques to how it was when it was first built.
He added the home would be rebuilt in Wallingford, but a location is being finalized and not ready to be announced.
The trust plans to use the reconstructed homestead as another museum and learning space, similar to two of its other properties – the Franklin Johnson Mansion, used as the American Silver Museum, and the Nehemiah Royce House, the oldest home in Wallingford.
“The Preservation Trust has extensive collections of items related to Wallingford history – we try to have them on display at the Nehemiah Royce House – but this will give us additional room to narrate and interpret Wallingford's history,” Farrell said.
The Yale building has eight rooms across its two stories. Farrell said he was surprised by how much original material from the structure was still intact, which has been preserved and will be reincorporated into the reconstruction.
Cicarella said the investment in the Yale Homestead was important for its preservation. It also prevents the materials from being worn down more while sitting in the trailers and causing the repairs or renovations to cost more down the road, he said.
The WHPT is also steward of a second disassembled historic building, the Muddy River Schoolhouse, a one-room school smaller than the Yale Homestead.
Farrell said that once the Yale Homestead was finished, they would likely begin looking at where and how the school would be restored, likely with the solicitation of smaller private donations.
The bond commission also awarded $6.8 million to assist Wallingford and other communities with post-closure care of local landfills.
